n: God summons priests, people, and the royal household to judgment. Their leaders have been like hunters’ traps at Mizpah and Mount Tabor—places where people were lured into false worship.

f.g: Probably Mizpah in Gilead, a site of corrupt worship.
A prominent mountain in Galilee, likely a shrine site.

n: The rebels have sunk deep into slaughter, yet God has repeatedly corrected them. The Hebrew here is difficult; it may refer to pagan sacrifices or to political violence.

f.w: the revolters are profound to make slaughter
f.g: The rebels are deep in slaughter; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: God knows Ephraim completely; nothing is hidden from Him. Israel is defiled by unfaithfulness.

f.w: Israel is not hid from me

n: Their actions don’t allow them to return to God, because a spirit of unfaithfulness rules them and they don’t know the Lord. Habitual sin makes repentance harder.

f.w: They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God
f.g: Their deeds don’t permit them to return.

n: Israel’s pride testifies against it. Both Israel and Judah will stumble.

f.w: the pride of Israel doth testify to his face

n: They will come with flocks and herds to sacrifice, but won’t find the Lord—He has withdrawn. Ritual without repentance cannot reach Him.
They have betrayed the Lord and raised children who don’t know Him. A new moon festival (“a month”) will devour them and their fields.

f.g: Children raised outside the covenant, or illegitimate children—a picture of a faithless generation.
Possibly a new moon festival, or simply a short time.

n: Sound the alarm! The trumpet blasts warn towns in Benjamin—Gibeah, Ramah, and Bethel—of invasion. These towns lay on the border between Israel and Judah.

f.g: Shofar—a ram’s-horn trumpet used to signal alarm.

n: Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of punishment. God has made it certain among the tribes.
Judah’s leaders are like people who move boundary stones—stealing land. God will pour out His wrath like a flood.

f.g: Those who move property markers to steal land.

n: Ephraim is crushed in judgment because it was determined to follow worthless commands—human-made rules or idols instead of God’s word.

f.g: Possibly “vanity” or “filth” in the Hebrew—worthless idols or human decrees.

n: God will be like a moth to Ephraim and rot to Judah—slow, unseen decay eating away at them from within.
When they felt their sickness, they turned to Assyria and its “great king” for help instead of to God. But Assyria couldn’t heal them. King Menahem of Israel paid tribute to Assyria around 740 BC.

f.g: Probably “the great king”—a title, not a name.

n: God Himself will attack like a lion, tearing and carrying off prey, with no one to rescue. The deeper message: the Lord, not Assyria, controls their fate.

f.w: I will be unto Ephraim as a lion

n: God will withdraw to His place until they admit their guilt and seek His face. In their distress they will earnestly seek Him. God waits with purpose, longing for their return.

f.w: till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face
